conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. __ from the bariatric surgery team. I hear you’re back because of severe pain around your G-tube site. Can you tell me what’s been happening since you went home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It never really got better. The pain around the tube keeps getting worse, and today it was so bad I couldn’t make it to clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’re dealing with this. Any fevers or chills? Any change in how the skin looks around the tube—more redness, swelling, or drainage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever or chills. It looks the same to me. It just hurts a lot, like deep and sharp.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Are you still tolerating your tube feeds at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been running them continuously—about 40 an hour. I’m always nauseated, but that’s not new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You were seen in the pain clinic yesterday, and they thought the pain might be from inflammation or a reaction around the tube, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. They said maybe it needs to be removed or replaced. But they didn’t change my meds, and the oxycodone isn’t touching it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. We’re going to focus on two things tonight: making sure there’s no infection or collection around the tube, and getting your pain under control. Your last CT showed inflammation around the tube but no abscess or hematoma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not infected? Why does it hurt this much then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Even without infection, the tissue and muscle around the tube can get inflamed and very sensitive—especially if it’s been irritated repeatedly. That can cause severe pain. We’ll examine the site closely and monitor you for any signs of infection while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In the ED we can try a steroid medication through the G-tube to see if it calms the inflammation locally. It doesn’t always work, but it’s a reasonable first step. Are you okay with us trying that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ll try anything. I just can’t go home like this again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did the steroid trial through the tube. How does the pain feel now—any change at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Maybe a tiny bit, but honestly it still really hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given that minimal response, we’re going to admit you overnight to manage the pain and nutrition safely. We’ll start with oral pain medication and adjust to what works best for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Does that mean surgery? Are you taking the tube out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No surgery is planned during this admission. Tonight the goal is symptom control and making sure your feeds and blood sugars are stable. Decisions about removing or replacing the tube are best made with your surgeon in follow-up, unless something urgent comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: we gave you oxycodone, but you’re still uncomfortable. We’d like to switch to oral hydromorphone—Dilaudid—because some patients get better relief with it. Does that sound okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’m nervous about strong meds, but I need something that works.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely reasonable. We’ll use the lowest effective dose, keep it as-needed, and also keep you on your bowel regimen to prevent constipation. And no driving or operating machinery while taking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night after switching to Dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. It’s not gone, but it’s finally manageable. I slept a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it helped. From our exams, the tube site looks stable—tender, but no signs of spreading redness or drainage, and you’ve had no fevers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also tried changing your feeding schedule to bolus feeds to see if that would be easier at home. Unfortunately, your blood sugar dropped after each bolus, which fits with your post-bypass hypoglycemia history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s what I was afraid of. I felt shaky and sweaty. So I can’t do bolus at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. For safety, we’re switching you back to continuous tube feeds. We’ll send you home on NutriHep at 50 cc per hour, and you should keep checking your blood sugars like you’ve been doing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home? I’m worried I’ll miss something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Come back or call right away for fever over 101.5, shaking chills, worsening redness or drainage at the tube site, vomiting where you can’t keep down fluids or meds, black or bloody stools or vomit, chest pain, shortness of breath, or if the pain is getting worse or changing location.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Dilaudid—how long will I have it? I don’t want to run out and end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you with a short course: hydromorphone 2 mg tablets to take by mouth every 4 hours as needed for pain, with a limited quantity. The plan is for you to follow up with your surgeon and your pain team to decide next steps for the tube and longer-term pain control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do I keep all my other meds the same? The anxiety meds and everything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—resume your regular home medications as before, including your fluoxetine, aripiprazole, and lorazepam, plus your ulcer protection meds like lansoprazole and sucralfate. Just be careful because lorazepam and Dilaudid together can make you extra sleepy—take them only as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go: you’re afebrile, your vitals are stable, you’re walking independently, and your pain is controlled on the oral regimen. We’ll discharge you home on continuous tube feeds at 50 cc/hr and the as-needed Dilaudid. Do you feel comfortable with the plan and the return precautions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I’m still worried about the tube pain coming back, but I understand the plan and I’ll follow up with my surgeon.
